                • 1. Selection caveat (the one provisional thing)
                • 2. Run inventory
                • 3. Fold → regime context (shared by all campaigns)
                • 4. Campaign 1 — Hand Sweep (2026-06-18/19)
                  • 4.1 Inputs
                  • 4.2 Method note — the comparison metric
                  • 4.3 Findings
                    • 4.3.1 The winner and the loser are the same in every regime
                    • 4.3.2 Mean net PnL per fold × config
                    • 4.3.3 The trailing-stop's harm is regime-dependent (the headline)
                    • 4.3.4 The take-profit lift also helps most where price oscillates up
                    • 4.3.5 How much the configuration matters is itself regime-dependent
                    • 4.3.6 Operational-counter mechanism (verified) — why the trailing stop churns
                  • 4.4 Conclusions
                  • 4.5 Caveats
                • 5. Campaign 2 — Optuna Pilot (2026-06-19)
                  • 5.1 Inputs
                  • 5.2 Method note
                  • 5.3 Findings
                    • 5.3.1 Optuna improved every trial — and turned one profitable
                    • 5.3.2 The optimum is regime-dependent (confirms the sweep)
                    • 5.3.3 Positive composite only in the bear folds
                    • 5.3.4 Parameter importance
                  • 5.4 Conclusions
                  • 5.5 Caveats
                • 6. Campaign 3 — Full Optuna Campaign (2026-06-22/24)
                  • 6.1 Inputs
                  • 6.2 Method note
                  • 6.3 Findings
                    • 6.3.1 Config tuning turns most losing trials profitable — in-sample
                    • 6.3.2 The winning config: stop-loss wide, take-profit high, trailing off-or-loose
                    • 6.3.3 The take-profit optimum is NOT regime-conditional at scale
                    • 6.3.4 Selectivity: winners trade little
                    • 6.3.5 Best (model, config) per fold
                    • 6.3.6 Top-5 trials per family — canonical Orig / New / Δ
                      • logistic — top 5 by New PnL
                      • mlp — top 5 by New PnL
                      • mlp_ex — top 5 by New PnL
                      • tcn — top 5 by New PnL
                      • vit — top 5 by New PnL
                    • 6.3.7 PnL-positive is not the same as alpha-positive
                    • 6.3.8 Coherence with the labeling service (why trailing-off wins)
                  • 6.4 Conclusions
                  • 6.5 Caveats
                • 7. Campaign 4 — Cross-Fold Transfer Validation (2026-06-24)
                  • 7.1 Inputs
                  • 7.2 Findings
                    • 7.2.1 Transfer matrix — mean New net PnL (config × target fold)
                    • 7.2.2 Share of trials with New PnL > 0
                    • 7.2.3 Mean New α (RC) — corrected benchmark
                  • 7.3 Conclusions

    Script 2 — Bot-Config Optimization: Consolidated Audit

    Created: 2026-06-29

    Predecessor documents in BOT_CONFIG/DEPRECATED/:

    • 20260619_SCRIPT2_BOT_CONFIG_01_HAND_SWEEP_AUDIT.md — hand sweep (Campaign 1)
    • 20260619_SCRIPT2_BOT_CONFIG_02_OPTUNA_PILOT_AUDIT.md — Optuna pilot (Campaign 2)
    • 20260624_SCRIPT2_BOT_CONFIG_03_OPTUNA_CAMPAIGN_AUDIT.md — full Optuna campaign (Campaign 3)
    • 20260624_SCRIPT2_BOT_CONFIG_04_CROSSFOLD_TRANSFER_AUDIT.md — cross-fold transfer (Campaign 4)

    All canonical campaign reports were regenerated 2026-06-30 12:27 UTC, after the risk-constrained benchmark was corrected for the last_price valuation bug (which followed the 2026-06-25 ATR-resolution backfill). Every result value here — both Orig (the baseline session) and New (the rerun) — is read from those regenerated reports / the corrected database.

    Reads: fold/regime context from AUDIT/REGIME/20260612_SCRIPT2_REGIME_FOLD_CROSSFOLD_FULL_AUDIT.md and AUDIT/REGIME/20260613_SCRIPT2_CROSS_FOLD_FAMILY_DIAGNOSTIC_AUDIT.md; campaign plan in docs/plans/THESIS-SCRIPT2/20260621_SCRIPT2_BOT_CONFIG_OPTIMIZATION_CAMPAIGN_PLAN.md; risk-constrained benchmark backfill bug in docs/audit/20260624_RC_BENCHMARK_BACKFILL_WRONG_ATR_AUDIT.md.

    This audit covers the complete bot-config optimization investigation: a 6-point hand sweep over the trailing/take-profit settings; a per-trial Optuna pilot; a full large-scale Optuna campaign across all four folds and five model families; and cross-fold transfer validation. The central question: can the right trailing-stop / take-profit / stop-loss configuration turn losing trials profitable, and does the winning recipe transfer across market regimes?

    1. Selection caveat (the one provisional thing)

    ⚠️ All four campaigns chose which trials to study by ranking on backtest_alpha_risk_constrained as it was stored at selection time — before the risk-constrained-benchmark backfill was corrected. That stored value was wrong: the backfill had used the input high price as the ATR, so the stored benchmark ≈ 0 and the stored alpha_rc collapsed onto the trial's return (see docs/audit/20260624_RC_BENCHMARK_BACKFILL_WRONG_ATR_AUDIT.md). The selection is therefore effectively a return ranking, not the intended risk-constrained-alpha ranking — with the corrected benchmark the ranking would differ, so potentially better candidates were left out. Re-select by the corrected alpha-RC before any further scaling.

    This affects only which trials were studied. The result values throughout this audit are on the corrected benchmark: the reports were regenerated on 2026-06-30 (after the last_price benchmark fix, which followed the 2026-06-25 ATR-resolution backfill), and the renderer re-sources every Orig (baseline) and New (rerun) session fresh from the corrected database, so both sides sit on the same correct basis and the Δ columns are like-for-like. The numbers are not contaminated — only the upstream choice of trials is provisional.

    4. Campaign 1 — Hand Sweep (2026-06-18/19)

    4.1 Inputs

    Source What it is
    bot_config_optimizer/requests/20260618_185125_highSL_trailing_tp_sweep.json The selection + 6-config sweep request (the primary evidence).
    run …/results/20260618_185125_highSL_trailing_tp_sweep/ 32 trials × 6 configs = 192 reruns; the canonical report.
    run …/results/20260618_181056_minitest_asis_vs_disabled/ 4 best-per-fold trials × {as-is, trailing-off}; the determinism control.
    runs …_minitest_best_per_fold / …_minitest_trailing_disabled Earlier 4-trial mini-tests.

    Selection of the 32: stage-3 baseline COMPLETED, stop_loss_exit_ratio ≥ 0.7 (stop-loss-heavy), top-8 per fold by alpha_risk_constrained (the stored value at selection time, see Section 1), diverse across tiers A+B and families LOG/MLP/MEX/TCN/VIT/AXV.

    The 6 configs (override on each trial's tier-template bot config; baseline trailing = atr, activation 3.0, distance 1.5, take-profit = risk_reward 2.0):

    Label Trailing Take-profit
    off_tp2 off 2.0
    current distance 1.5, activation 3.0 2.0
    wide_tp2 distance 3.0 2.0
    wide_tp3 distance 3.0 3.0
    wider_tp3 distance 5.0 3.0
    off_tp3 off 3.0

    4.2 Method note — the comparison metric

    The six configs are compared on net PnL. The question this sweep answers is which trailing / take-profit setting produces more money per trial, and net PnL is the direct economic answer: all six configs run on the same trials, so their PnL ordering is the finding. The risk-constrained alpha_rc is available on every session and on the corrected benchmark, but it is not the discriminator here. All numbers below are the mean over the 8 trials in each fold, for the rerun session.

    4.3 Findings

    4.3.1 The winner and the loser are the same in every regime

    off_tp3 (no trailing, take-profit 3.0) has the best mean PnL in all four folds; current (the deployed trailing, distance 1.5) has the worst in all four. Across the full 32-trial set off_tp3 wins 22/32 trials and is the only config with any positive-PnL trials (2, both in F1).

    4.3.2 Mean net PnL per fold × config

    Config F1 chop F2 bull F3 bear F4 bear-mixed
    off_tp3 −$181.8 −$238.3 −$188.6 −$223.3
    wider_tp3 −$318.8 −$343.9 −$229.1 −$233.0
    off_tp2 (≈ baseline) −$338.6 −$332.2 −$244.6 −$251.2
    wide_tp3 −$476.7 −$443.6 −$271.4 −$292.0
    wide_tp2 −$479.1 −$487.2 −$290.6 −$312.3
    current −$617.4 −$523.7 −$310.9 −$363.1
    baseline −$338.6 −$332.2 −$244.6 −$251.2

    off_tp2 reproduces the baseline exactly in every fold — identical per-trial net PnL and trade count (e.g. F1 trial 680: −$249 and 74 trades on both sides). The baseline stage-3 sessions therefore carry no trailing-stop exits; current is the same take-profit with the trailing active at distance 1.5, and it is the trailing firing that adds the churn. The exact match is also the determinism control: re-applying a config that produces no trailing exits reproduces the baseline trade-for-trade.

    4.3.3 The trailing-stop's harm is regime-dependent (the headline)

    Isolating the trailing stop (current − off_tp2, both take-profit 2.0):

    Fold Regime Trailing "tax" (mean PnL) Trade-count inflation (off → current)
    F1 Ranging / chop −$278.8 (worst) 190.6 → 281.8 (+48%)
    F2 Clean bull −$191.4 173.0 → 222.1 (+28%)
    F3 Trending bear −$66.3 (mildest) 79.5 → 107.9 (+36%)
    F4 Mixed bear −$111.9 86.4 → 117.6 (+36%)

    The trailing stop does ~4× more damage in the ranging fold (F1) than in the trending-bear fold (F3). The mechanism is whipsaw: in a directionless / choppy market price oscillates through the trailing band repeatedly, closing positions early and forcing re-entries (F1 churns the most extra trades). In a clean down-trend the trailing is hit cleanly with less oscillation, so it churns less and costs less.

    4.3.4 The take-profit lift also helps most where price oscillates up

    Isolating the take-profit (off_tp3 − off_tp2, both trailing off):

    Fold Regime Take-profit benefit (2.0 → 3.0)
    F1 Ranging / chop +$156.8 (best)
    F2 Clean bull +$93.9
    F3 Trending bear +$56.1
    F4 Mixed bear +$27.9 (smallest)

    Raising the take-profit captures larger up-swings before they revert; that pays most in the chop and bull folds (F1/F2, where up-moves exist to capture) and least in the strong-bear fold (F4, fewest up-moves).

    4.3.5 How much the configuration matters is itself regime-dependent

    The PnL swing from worst (current) to best (off_tp3) per fold:

    Fold Regime PnL swing (worst → best)
    F1 Ranging / chop $435.6
    F2 Clean bull $285.4
    F3 Trending bear $122.4
    F4 Mixed bear $139.8

    Configuration choice swings outcomes ~3.5× more in the ranging fold than in the trending-bear fold. The stakes of getting trailing/TP right are highest in choppy markets.

    4.3.6 Operational-counter mechanism (verified) — why the trailing stop churns

    The reruns populate the operational gate counters; the baseline stage-3 sessions do not carry them. The counters are internally coherent: candidates = attempts + proposal_blocked, entry_blocked = proposal_blocked + (attempts − approved), and approved = positions opened (closed trades plus any still open at the window end). Same trial (F1, 2391), same predictions (3,758 candidate signals either way):

    Run Trades Candidates Proposal-blocked Attempts Approved Risk-blocked Approval rate
    trailing OFF (9195) 154 3758 1831 1927 157 1770 8.1%
    trailing ON (9191) 262 3758 2575 1183 263 920 22.2%

    The model emits the same candidate signals both ways; the difference is slot turnover. The trailing stop closes positions early (in 9191: 82 TRAILING_STOP exits, 121 trades trailed), so max_concurrent_positions slots free up more often and the risk manager approves a far higher share of entries (22% vs 8%), opening 263 vs 157 positions. With trailing off, positions ride to stop-loss / take-profit, slots stay occupied, and the risk manager blocks far more entries on the position cap (1,770 vs 920), so the bot opens fewer. The extra entries also trigger more post-entry cooldown windows, which raises the pre-risk proposal_blocked count. No risk halts or force-flats fire in this fold (both counters 0), so the churn is entirely the trailing-exit → free-slot → re-entry loop, not risk-manager intervention. This is the operational reason the trailing stop both exits more and enters more.

    4.4 Conclusions

    1. Confirmed: the trailing / take-profit configuration interacts with regime. The trailing stop is most harmful in ranging and bull folds (whipsaw) and least harmful in the trending-bear fold; the take-profit lift helps most in chop/bull and least in strong bear.
    2. The deployed trailing config (distance 1.5) is the worst option in every regime and should be widened or disabled. Across all 32 trials and all four regimes, no trailing + higher take-profit is the best of the tested configs.
    3. None of this turns the strategy profitable. Every config is negative-mean in every fold; only off_tp3 produces any positive trials (2/32, both in F1). These are stop-loss-heavy trials by selection; tuning trailing/TP reduces the loss, it does not create an edge.

    4.5 Caveats

    • Stop-loss was not varied (held at atr 2.5). The SL × regime interaction is untested; it is the obvious next lever, especially since the selection targeted stop-loss-heavy trials.
    • Stop-loss-heavy selection (stop_loss_exit_ratio ≥ 0.7) biases toward losers; the whole candidate pool is stop-loss-heavy (1025/1026 trials ≥ 0.5), so this is representative of the population, but the configs were not tested on the rare non-stop-loss-heavy trials.
    • The sweep reads net PnL across the six configs. The risk-constrained alpha is available per session on the corrected benchmark but is not the sweep's discriminator; the per-trial alpha pattern is read in Campaign 3 (Section 6.3.7).
    • Hand-picked configs, not a search. Six points in {trailing distance, trailing enabled, take-profit}; the optima between them are unprobed.
    • Reruns are strategy-identical to the baseline, not bit-identical. A field-by-field check (scripts/tmp_utils/checks/compare_backtest_sessions.py, baseline session 1218 vs trailing-off rerun 9195) confirms all 157 trades match the baseline trade-for-trade (side, size, entry/exit price, PnL, gross PnL, commissions, exit reason within 1e-9). Predictions are re-inferred per run, so model confidences differ at ~1e-7 (float, non-decision-flipping); that shifts ref_gross (~$0.5/trade) and a few session-tail aggregates (last price, exposure, slippage, daily volatility). The risk-constrained benchmark family and the operational counters differ as expected (recomputed / not carried on the baseline). Trade decisions are unaffected, which is why the trailing-off rerun reproduces the baseline economics exactly.

    5. Campaign 2 — Optuna Pilot (2026-06-19)

    5.1 Inputs

    Source What it is
    bot_config_optimizer/requests/optuna_regime_trailing_tp_sl.json The selection + Optuna search request.
    run …/results/20260619_040950_optuna_regime_trailing_tp_sl/ 8 studies × 40 trials = 320 backtests; per-study optuna_trial_<id>.sqlite, results.json, report.

    Selection: stage-3 baseline COMPLETED, stop_loss_exit_ratio ≥ 0.7, top-2 per fold by alpha_risk_constrained (the stored value at selection time, see Section 1) → 8 trials, 2 per regime: F1 LOG+MEX, F2 VIT+VIT, F3 VIT+VIT, F4 MEX+VIT.

    Search space: trailing_stop.distance (1–6), trailing_stop.activation (1–6), take_profit.value (1–4), stop_loss.value (1–4).

    Objective: 0.5·alpha_rc + 0.5·return_pct (weighted-mean composite). 40 TPE trials per studied trial, seed 42.

    5.2 Method note

    The composite objective blends the risk-constrained alpha with the raw return so the TPE sampler has a usable gradient across a stop-loss-heavy population. Within one study every config runs on the same trial, so the search ranking is internally consistent; the baseline-vs-best comparison below reads net PnL, the economic bottom line.

    5.3 Findings

    5.3.1 Optuna improved every trial — and turned one profitable

    Best Optuna config per trial vs the trial's baseline:

    Regime Model Best PnL Baseline PnL Best config act / dist / TP / SL
    F1 chop mlp_ex +$306 −$316 4.9 / 4.9 / 3.9 / 4.0
    F1 chop logistic −$195 −$249 6.0 / 3.0 / 3.5 / 3.5
    F2 bull vit −$53 −$235 4.5 / 4.9 / 3.5 / 3.9
    F2 bull vit −$111 −$266 3.7 / 5.3 / 3.5 / 3.8
    F3 bear vit −$10 −$216 3.1 / 6.0 / 1.4 / 4.0
    F3 bear vit −$68 −$110 3.8 / 6.0 / 1.0 / 3.7
    F4 bear-mix vit −$130 −$194 4.0 / 6.0 / 3.6 / 3.3
    F4 bear-mix mlp_ex −$86 −$96 5.7 / 1.3 / 3.9 / 3.4

    Every one of the 8 trials improved on its baseline; F1 mlp_ex flipped from −$316 to +$306 — the first profitable result in this line of work.

    5.3.2 The optimum is regime-dependent (confirms the sweep)

    • Take-profit: high (3.5–3.9) in the chop/bull folds (F1, F2) and the mixed-bear F4, but low (1.0–1.4) in the clean trending-bear F3 — take small gains quickly in a downtrend, let them run in chop/up. (Note: this per-regime split does not survive at full scale — see Section 6.3.3.)
    • Stop-loss: wide (3.3–4.0) everywhere — wider stops avoid the premature exits that dominate this stop-loss-heavy population.
    • Trailing: wide (distance ≈ 5–6, effectively off) in 7 of 8 — consistent with the sweep finding that a tight trailing stop only churns and hurts. (One F4 outlier used distance 1.3.)

    5.3.3 Positive composite only in the bear folds

    The composite objective is positive only for F3/F4; F1/F2 stay negative — the defensive edge concentrates in down markets, matching the regime audit, and Campaign 3 confirms this at the per-trial alpha level (Section 6.3.7).

    5.3.4 Parameter importance

    Across the studies, take_profit.value and stop_loss.value dominate the Optuna importance; the trailing parameters matter less. Adding the stop-loss to the search was the decisive lever.

    5.4 Conclusions

    1. An Optuna search beats the hand-picked configs and tunes per trial, improving all 8 and producing one profitable trial — the apparatus and the composite objective work end to end.
    2. The optimal config appears regime-conditional at this scale, chiefly through the take-profit: high in chop/bull, low in trending bear; the stop-loss is best wide and the trailing stop best loose/off in every regime.
    3. Stop-loss and take-profit are the dominant levers here, not the trailing stop.

    5.5 Caveats

    • Per-trial reruns on a stop-loss-heavy selection; the headline is net PnL.
    • 40 trials per study is a modest budget; the optima are indicative, not converged.
    • The single profitable result (F1 mlp_ex) is in-sample to its fold; it must be validated out-of-fold before it means anything.
    • The per-regime take-profit split observed here (low in F3) is a small-sample artifact — it does not generalize to the full population at scale (see Section 6.3.3).

    6. Campaign 3 — Full Optuna Campaign (2026-06-22/24)

    6.1 Inputs

    Source What it is
    bot_config_optimizer/requests/20260622_etapa1_<family>.json Five per-family search requests.
    …/results/20260622_*_etapa1_{logistic,mlp,mlp_ex,tcn,vit}/ optuna_trial_<id>.sqlite, results.json / .csv, report.md.

    Selection: top-5 trials per (family, fold) ranked by backtest_alpha_risk_constrained (the stored value at selection time, see Section 1), over the five canonical source runs (20260319_035820, 20260323_tierA_rescue_v2, 20260325_tierB_mlp_ex, 20260328_tierB_corrected, 20260401_tierB_rescue_v5). Families logistic, mlp, mlp_ex, tcn, vit; 20 trials each → 100 trials, 25 per fold.

    Search space: trailing_stop.enabled (on/off), trailing_stop.distance (1–6), trailing_stop.activation (1–6), take_profit.value (1–4), stop_loss.value (1–4).

    Objective: 0.5·return_pct + 0.5·alpha_risk_constrained (weighted composite). 30 TPE trials per study, seed 42, no pruning (the reruns are MANUAL backtests, which run the full validation window). 3,000 backtests total.

    6.2 Method note

    One independent Optuna study per studied trial: each trial is a different trained model with its own cached predictions, so its best config is a separate optimization problem (pooling trials would feed the TPE sampler incomparable objective values). Each study fully searches its trial's config space; the per-trial study is stored in its own sqlite for independence, resume, and audit.

    Orig is the trial's baseline stage-3 session; New is the tuned-config rerun. Both sessions read their risk-constrained benchmark from the corrected database (the renderer re-sources each side fresh from backtest_sessions by id), so Orig α (RC) and New α (RC) are on the same corrected basis and Δ α (RC) is a like-for-like comparison. The baseline and rerun benchmarks agree to ~1–2 pp; small per-session residuals remain because each session's benchmark is computed over its own execution window with the live ATR. The best config is the maximum over 30 searched configs on the trial's own fold, so every number here is in-sample and optimistic by construction.

    6.3 Findings

    6.3.1 Config tuning turns most losing trials profitable — in-sample

    68 of 100 trials have a PnL-positive best config. It works in every fold, including the two folds that never produced a profitable trial before:

    Fold Regime Best config PnL > 0 Baseline PnL > 0 Median Δ PnL
    F1 ranging 23/25 8/25 +$494
    F2 bull 11/25 0/25 +$456
    F3 bear 15/25 6/25 +$264
    F4 bear-mix 19/25 0/25 +$489

    F2 and F4 go from zero baseline-profitable trials to 11/25 and 19/25 — config alone, no retrain.

    6.3.2 The winning config: stop-loss wide, take-profit high, trailing off-or-loose

    • Trailing: of the 100 winning configs, 46 disable it, 42 keep it but wide (distance ≥ 4.5), only 12 keep it tight (distance < 4.5) — 88/100 are off-or-loose. The tight-trailing churn that dominated the deployed config is almost never optimal.
    • Stop-loss: median 3.68 (range 1.90–3.99) — wide, as in the earlier sweep.
    • Take-profit: median 3.45 (range 1.06–4.00) — high.

    6.3.3 The take-profit optimum is NOT regime-conditional at scale

    Per-fold median take-profit is essentially flat — F1 3.55, F2 3.47, F3 3.41, F4 3.42 — i.e. high in the bear folds too. This revises the single-run pilot (Section 5), which read take-profit as low (1.0–1.4) in the trending-bear fold. With a real budget across many trials the take-profit optimum is uniformly high; the earlier per-regime split does not generalize. Median stop-loss is similarly wide across folds (F1 3.53, F2 3.72, F3 3.56, F4 3.89), and loose trailing was already regime-flat.

    6.3.4 Selectivity: winners trade little

    The median trade count of the PnL-positive winners is 72 — at or below the ~100–150 selectivity zone flagged as the primary economic lever. The configs that win do so by trading less.

    F2 mlp_ex 2256 −$463 → +$365 trailing off, TP 3.37, SL 3.97, 30 trades

    6.3.7 PnL-positive is not the same as alpha-positive

    With the corrected benchmark the regime split is visible already in the baseline and sharpens after tuning:

    • In the rising-benchmark folds (F1 +11.9%, F2 +4.2%) the baseline trials sit at strongly negative α (RC) (−10% to −17% in F1) because they barely move while buy-and-hold rises. Tuning lifts α by +3 to +11 pp, but it stays negative: the winners make money yet still underperform the deploying benchmark. The headline mlp 3167 makes +$952 (+9.5%) and lifts α from −13.4% to −2.4% — a large improvement, but −2.4% against a +11.9% benchmark is still a miss.
    • In the falling-benchmark folds (F3 −6.9%, F4 −8.4%) the winners are both PnL-positive and α(RC)-positive (+10% to +13%): they make money and beat the deploying benchmark (vit 7545 in F4: +$413 and +12.6% RC alpha, up from a baseline +8.3%; logistic 797 in F4: +$454 and +13.0%, up from +5.2%). Because the corrected benchmark deploys ≈ 60% of equity, this is not an under-deployment artifact — the defensive bear-fold edge is real at the single-trial level and now carries positive absolute PnL. This is the strongest single-trial signal in this line so far, still in-sample.

    6.3.8 Coherence with the labeling service (why trailing-off wins)

    The labels are ATR-based (config/experiments/labeling.yaml, threshold_type: atr_based): a LONG is labeled when price rises ≥ up_threshold = 5 × ATR without first drawing down more than max_drawdown_before_up = 2 × ATR. A valid labeled move therefore targets 5 × ATR and tolerates a 2 × ATR adverse excursion on the way.

    The deployed bot config is calibrated to that on price levels: stop-loss 2.5 × ATR, take-profit risk_reward 2.0 → 5 × ATR (= the labeled target). The piece that broke the coherence was the deployed trailing stop at distance 1.5 × ATR — tighter than the 2 × ATR retracement a valid move tolerates, so it closed winners before they reached the 5 × ATR target. This is the mechanism behind the empirical result that trailing-off (or wide) wins: a trailing tighter than the labeled tolerance is structurally guaranteed to cut labeled moves short.

    If a trailing stop is kept on, the labeling-coherent floor is distance ≥ 2 × ATR (never below the labeled tolerance); distance 2.5 × ATR (= the initial stop) with activation ≈ 3 × ATR keeps it from ever sitting tighter than the entry risk while still protecting deep profit. Position sizing is independent of the labels — the labels set direction and move magnitude, not position size.

    6.4 Conclusions

    1. Config tuning is a strong in-sample lever. Across all regimes, the right trailing/TP/SL turns a majority of losing trials profitable — including the previously hopeless bull (F2) and mixed-bear (F4) folds.
    2. The recipe is consistent, not regime-specific: wide stop-loss, high take-profit, trailing off-or-loose, few trades. The earlier per-regime take-profit split does not survive at scale.
    3. The deployed tight trailing remains the wrong default — it is the optimum in only 12 of 100 trials.
    4. In the bear folds the per-trial edge is benchmark-beating (positive α RC), confirming at the single-trial level the defensive pattern the regime audits read at the ensemble level.

    6.5 Caveats

    • In-sample and optimistic. The best config is the max over 30 searched configs on each trial's own fold; the flip rate measures in-sample capability, not realized edge. It means nothing until the winning configs are validated on other folds.
    • Selection by the stored alpha_rc at selection time (Section 1): the studied population is provisional and likely missing better candidates. The per-trial reading itself is on the corrected benchmark and is sound.

    7.3 Conclusions

    1. The original (deployed) config loses in all four folds (−$126 / −$655 / −$122 / −$492). Every winning config beats it in every fold.
    2. The config recipe transfers. winner_F2 and winner_F3 are net-PnL-positive in all four folds (winner_F3 wins 17/20 trials across folds). This is the first cross-fold-transferring result in the project — it reproduces the campaign recipe (wide stop-loss, high take-profit, trailing off) and it is regime-robust, in contrast with the fold-local ensemble recipes.
    3. winner_F1 and winner_F4 fail the bull fold F2 (−$88, −$173), so not every winner transfers; the robust ones (winner_F2/winner_F3, both wide-SL / high-TP / trailing-off) do. F2 (clean bull) is the discriminator.
    4. The benchmark-beating edge (positive α RC) stays concentrated in the bear folds; bull folds remain negative-alpha (the strategy makes money but does not beat a deploying buy-and-hold).

    7.4 Caveats

    • Selection by the stored alpha_rc (see Section 1): the studied trials were ranked on that value, so the trial set is provisional and likely missing better candidates. Re-select after re-ranking by the corrected alpha-RC.
    • Strong trials only: transfer is shown on the top-5 trials per fold, not the whole population.
    • Bull-fold alpha is negative against the (≈ 60%-deployed) risk-constrained benchmark; read the PnL transfer as the headline and the alpha-RC as "versus a near-max-deployed passive benchmark".

    8. Cross-campaign synthesis

    8.1 The investigation arc

    The four campaigns formed a coherent progression of evidence:

    Campaign Scope Key question answered
    1 — Hand sweep 32 trials × 6 configs Does trailing/TP interact with regime? Yes — trailing harms most in chop (4×).
    2 — Optuna pilot 8 trials × 40 TPE Does search beat hand-picked? Yes — all 8 improved, first profitable result (+$306 F1).
    3 — Full campaign 100 trials × 30 TPE Does it scale? Yes — 68/100 turn profitable, recipe is uniform not regime-split.
    4 — Transfer 5 configs × 20 trials Does the recipe transfer? Yes — winner_F2/winner_F3 positive in all 4 folds (17/20 trials).

    8.2 Consolidated recipe

    The evidence across all four campaigns converges on the same config recipe:

    Parameter Finding Confidence
    Trailing stop enabled Off, or wide (distance ≥ 4.5 × ATR) Very high — 88/100 winners are off-or-loose; churn mechanism verified operationally (Section 4.3.6) and explained by label coherence (Section 6.3.8).
    Take-profit High (3.0–4.0 × ATR) High — consistent across all campaigns; the per-regime split (low in F3) observed in the pilot does not survive at scale.
    Stop-loss Wide (3.4–4.0 × ATR) High — wide stops win in every campaign and every fold without exception.
    Trade frequency Low (median ≈ 72 trades) High — winners trade less; the recipe reduces position churn from the trailing stop, which is the proximate cause of fewer trades.

    The best (model, config) per fold, on the corrected benchmark, in one comparable view (in-sample):

    Fold Regime Trial New PnL (Ret%) New Bm RC New α (RC) Winning recipe
    F1 ranging mlp 3167 +$952 (+9.5%) +11.9% −2.4% trailing off, TP 3.24, SL 3.47, 69 trades
    F2 bull mlp_ex 2256 +$365 (+3.6%) +4.2% −0.5% trailing off, TP 3.37, SL 3.97, 30 trades
    F3 bear vit 3955 +$354 (+3.5%) −6.9% +10.5% trailing off, TP 3.11, SL 3.99, 31 trades
    F4 bear-mix logistic 797 +$454 (+4.5%) −8.4% +13.0% trailing on (d6.0/a5.4), TP 3.93, SL 3.43, 98 trades

    In the rising-benchmark folds (F1/F2) the best config makes money but its α (RC) stays negative (it does not beat a deploying buy-and-hold); in the falling-benchmark folds (F3/F4) the best config is both PnL-positive and α (RC)-positive — the same defensive pattern the campaigns show throughout.

    8.3 The structural explanation

    The labeling service marks a LONG when price rises ≥ 5 × ATR without first drawing down > 2 × ATR. The deployed trailing at distance 1.5 × ATR is tighter than the labeled tolerance (2 × ATR), so it structurally exits valid labeled moves before the 5 × ATR target — guaranteed to underperform the labeled signal. The fix is architectural, not empirical: trailing must be either off or at distance ≥ 2 × ATR. The empirical campaigns confirmed this structural prediction across 3,000+ backtests.

    8.4 Transfer vs ensemble recipes

    The bot-config recipe (winner_F2/winner_F3) is the first cross-fold-transferring result in the project. The ensemble recipes from the Phase-1/Phase-3 cross-fold transfer campaigns were fold-local (12–14% positive off-fold trials at best). The bot-config recipe achieves 16–17/20 positive trials across all four folds simultaneously — a qualitatively different outcome.

    The two findings operate on different layers:

    • Ensemble recipe: which models to combine for a defensive alpha in bear folds. Fold-local.
    • Bot-config recipe: how to execute any model to reduce churn and improve raw PnL. Cross-fold transferring.

    Neither finding is out-of-sample in a held-out time window; both remain in-sample.

    8.5 What remains provisional

    1. Trial selection: all four campaigns chose trials by the stored alpha_rc at selection time, so the studied population is effectively ranked by return. With the corrected alpha-RC some trials may have higher priority. The recipe itself is likely robust (it was consistent across 100 trials), but the per-fold winners (especially the best single trial per fold) could change.
    2. Out-of-sample validation: every result is in-sample to the campaign's validation folds. A held- out window test is the next required step for any deployment claim.
    3. Population breadth: the hand sweep and pilot used stop_loss_exit_ratio ≥ 0.7 (stop-loss-heavy trials). The full campaign extended to all top-5 per fold; coverage of the rare profitable-baseline trial is thin.
    4. Ensemble × config interaction: the winning bot configs were searched per individual trial; whether the same recipe is optimal when applied to an ensemble combination is untested.

    8.6 Recommended next steps

    1. Re-select by corrected alpha-RC and re-run Campaign 3 (full Optuna) if the top-5 per fold change materially. Re-run Campaign 4 (transfer) with the new per-fold winners.
    2. Out-of-sample window test of winner_F2/winner_F3 style (SL ≈ 4.0, TP ≈ 3.4, trailing off) on a held-out time window not used in any fold.
    3. Ensemble × config joint search: apply the recipe to ensemble combinations rather than individual trials to test whether ensemble alpha and config PnL improvements are additive.
    4. Regime-conditional deployment guard: the bull-fold alpha-RC is persistently negative (−3.5% to −9.8% even with the best config); deploying the recipe in a confirmed-bull regime may still lose to the benchmark. A regime gate (deploy only in ranging/bear) could protect capital.
